# Accessing R

Please ensure that you have access to R. This can be a local version on your computer ([Warwick download link](https://anorien.csc.warwick.ac.uk/CRAN/)) or [online](https://noteable.edina.ac.uk).

If you have a local version, it is also worth downloading an IDE (integrated development environment). I personally use [RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/).

Whether you use R locally or in a browser-based environment, the most important thing is that you can run code, inspect the results, and save your work. This course is designed so the examples will work in both a simple R script and in a Quarto document.

## How to use this course

Each section is written as a mix of:

- short explanations of the key ideas,
- concrete code examples you can run,
- practical checks to test your understanding.

Start by reading the introductory pages, then run the examples yourself. When a page includes a “Check your understanding” exercise, try solving it before opening the answer.

The course is deliberately written for two readers at once. If you are **finding it hard**, stick to the core explanation and the code examples — you do not need to absorb every detail on the first pass. If you **already know the basics and want more**, watch for the green **"Going further" boxes**, which point to cooler packages, neater techniques and deeper ideas you can safely explore (or skip). See the [Welcome page](index.qmd) for a fuller description of how to read the course at your own level.

## Navigation tips

The course is organised by topic rather than by difficulty. If you are new to R, follow the **Introduction to R** section first. If you already know the basics, you can move directly to the **Theory of Programming**, **Mathematics to R**, **Linear modelling**, **Exploratory data analysis**, **Data Visualisation**, or **Report Writing** sections.

# Creating a new document

There are many possible files that you can create in R. The simplest is to create an R script. This allows you to write code, run code and produce output. You can also annotate your code through comments by writing `#` and then adding any relevant text.

Alternatively, you can create an R Markdown file. This combines chunks of R code with normal text. Thus, you can create lovely reports that blend code output (e.g. figures and tables) with analysis. There is a detailed [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/) getting-started guide on how to use these documents.
